heading: Why temporary staffing matters in London
body: Care services across Greater London face fluctuating demand, staff sickness and seasonal pressure. heading: The essentials
body: CQC compliance in staffing is about being able to show, with evidence, that you have enough suitably skilled people on shift to meet residents' needs safely. Regulation 18 of the Health and Social Care Act regulations sets the expectation for sufficient numbers of suitably qualified, competent and experienced staff. The single assessment framework then asks providers to evidence this through quality statements on an ongoing basis, rather than through one-off inspections.

heading: What's changing this quarter, at a glance
body: The direction of travel is towards continuous, evidence-led assurance. Inspectors increasingly expect to see planned staffing compared against actual staffing, clear supervision records, and up-to-date competency evidence for every worker, including agency staff. Providers who keep this evidence current throughout the year, rather than assembling it before an inspection, are far better placed. Building a light-touch quarterly refresh into your routine keeps records inspection-ready at all times.

heading: Interview and screening approach
body: A good interview explores values as well as experience. Ask candidates to describe how they have handled a difficult shift, supported a resident with dignity, or raised a safeguarding concern. Scenario-based questions reveal judgement far better than yes-or-no questions. Take structured notes so you can compare candidates fairly and evidence your decision later.

heading: Introduction
body: This statement sets out the steps Vigil Care Staffing takes to prevent modern slavery and human trafficking within our own operations and our supply chains. Modern slavery is a serious crime and a violation of fundamental human rights. We are committed to acting ethically and with integrity in all our business relationships, and to preventing modern slavery in any part of our activities. This statement is made in the spirit of the Modern Slavery Act 2015.

heading: Our business
body: Vigil Care Staffing supplies vetted care-sector workers, including healthcare assistants, support workers and healthcare cleaners, to care providers across Greater London. Because we recruit and place people, safer recruitment sits at the heart of how we protect workers from exploitation.

heading: Our commitment
body: We have zero tolerance for modern slavery. We expect the same high standards from everyone we work with, including the clients we supply and the partners who support our operations. We are committed to ensuring that no form of forced labour, servitude or human trafficking takes place within our business or our supply chains.

heading: Due diligence and our supply chains
body: We seek to understand and manage the risk of modern slavery in our supply chains. This includes taking care to work with reputable partners and being alert to the warning signs of exploitation. Where we identify a risk or concern, we act to address it promptly and appropriately.

heading: Safer recruitment and vetting
body: Our vetting process is a key safeguard against exploitation. We verify the identity and right to work of every worker, confirm references, and pay careful attention to indicators that a person may be at risk of modern slavery, such as controlled documents or wages paid to a third party. These checks help protect the workers we place as well as the people they care for.

heading: Training and awareness
body: We raise awareness of modern slavery among our team so that they can recognise the signs and know how to raise concerns. Building this understanding into our recruitment and day-to-day operations helps us respond quickly if a concern arises.

heading: Responsibility and review
body: Responsibility for this statement and for preventing modern slavery rests with the management of Vigil Care Staffing. We keep our approach under review and will update our practices and this statement as needed to reflect changes in our business or in good practice.

heading: Trained versus capable
body: A training certificate proves that a member of staff attended a course. It does not, on its own, prove that they can apply that learning safely in daily practice. Continuous professional development, or CPD, closes that gap. Well-planned CPD moves a team from simply being trained to being genuinely capable, and it produces the kind of evidence inspectors expect to see.

heading: A three-step framework for CQC-ready staff development
body: A dependable CPD programme does not have to be complicated. The following three steps give care home managers a repeatable cycle: identify the skills your service needs, embed learning in everyday work, and review the impact regularly. Each step builds evidence that your staffing supports safe, effective care.

heading: Mapping care home CPD to CQC quality statements
body: The CQC single assessment framework is built around quality statements grouped under themes such as safe, effective and well-led. Linking your CPD records to these statements shows how workforce development supports the outcomes inspectors assess. The examples below illustrate how everyday CPD activity can be mapped to those themes.

heading: Why residential care staffing in Havering is shifting
body: Havering is one of outer north-east London's larger boroughs, with an ageing population and a steady demand for residential care across Romford, Hornchurch, Upminster, Rainham, Elm Park, and Collier Row. That demand has grown faster than the local workforce, and managers increasingly find that the old model of calling a distant agency at the eleventh hour no longer holds up. The direction of travel in 2026 is towards locally rooted, values-based staffing: pools of vetted workers who know the area, can travel short distances, and can return to the same homes week after week. For a residential home, the aim is no longer simply to fill a gap on the rota, but to fill it with someone reliable who fits the culture of the service and the needs of its residents.

heading: The financial reality: budgeting for 2026
body: Staffing is the single largest cost in most residential homes, and 2026 brings continued pressure from national living wage increases and strong competition for experienced carers across east London. Budgeting well means planning for realistic agency rates rather than hoping to fill gaps at the lowest possible price, because the cheapest cover often carries the highest hidden cost in turnover, retraining, and quality risk. A sensible 2026 plan sets a clear budget line for temporary cover, tracks how often it is used, and weighs the price of a shift against the value of continuity and safe staffing levels. Transparent, agreed rates make this far easier: when you know the cost of cover in advance, you can protect both your budget and your standards. Vigil Care Staffing works to clear, transparent rates so there are no surprises on the invoice.

heading: CQC readiness: evidence categories for staffing
body: Inspectors want to see that a home is safely and consistently staffed, and that the evidence to prove it is easy to produce. For staffing, the categories that matter most are safe staffing records that show planned versus actual numbers on every shift, training and competency records for the people who worked, and vetting evidence such as DBS checks, right-to-work documents, and references for any temporary workers used. Supervision and induction records show that agency staff were properly briefed before caring for residents, while feedback and incident logs demonstrate that quality was monitored throughout. Keeping this evidence current and organised turns an inspection from a scramble into a straightforward review. A good staffing partner helps by supplying compliant, fully documented workers whose paperwork slots neatly into your own records.

heading: What cookies are
body: Cookies (and similar technologies like local storage) are small files a website can store on your device. Some are essential to make the site work; others are non-essential (such as analytics) and, by law, require your consent before they can be set.

heading: Cookies this website uses

If you accept analytics, Google Analytics 4 sets its measurement cookies (‘_ga’ and ‘_ga_*’) to measure site usage so we can improve the site; these last up to two years (Google’s default). We do not use advertising, marketing, re-targeting or social-media tracking cookies, or any unrelated third-party tracking, and we keep Google’s advertising features (‘Google signals’) switched off.

body: On your first visit you will see a banner with Accept and Reject presented equally. Nothing non-essential loads until you choose.
